About

Research
Overview

I am a fifth-year PhD candidate in the Coon Lab at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, advised by Professor Joshua J. Coon.

My research is centered on analytical method development and the application of multi-omics to biological discovery. I work to push mass spectrometry to new limits in sensitivity, coverage, throughput, and reproducibility — and to deploy these tools toward understanding aging, metabolism, and disease.

Before Madison, I earned a B.Sc. in Molecular & Cell Biology (minors in Bioinformatics and Chemistry) from The American University in Cairo, and trained as an undergraduate researcher at Egypt's Children's Cancer Hospital 57357, where my work spanned cancer biology and the proteomics of ancient Egyptian archaeological materials.

Beyond the lab bench, I have contributed to graduate admissions (IPiB), the USAID and Egyptian Ministry of Education Merit-Based Scholarship, and mentoring initiatives that support researchers from diverse backgrounds. Outside the lab, I enjoy cooking new recipes, pencil sketching, and exploring new hobbies.

Research

Datasets &
Projects

Longitudinal Multi-Omics of Aging & Caloric Restriction in Rhesus Macaques

Longitudinal proteomics, metabolomics, and lipidomics profiling of nearly 500 plasma samples collected over three decades from rhesus macaques. Investigates molecular signatures of aging, sex-dependent metabolic differences, and the effects of caloric restriction on age-related metabolic remodeling.

→ Mol. Systems Biology, 2025  ·  Science, 2026 (under review)

Multi-Omic Analysis of Post-Acute Sequelae of COVID-19

Integrated proteomics, lipidomics, and transcriptomics analysis of post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC). Built a curated molecular database and applied statistical modeling to identify multi-omic signatures associated with distinct long COVID clinical manifestations.

→ Scientific Reports, 2026

OptiSpray–μPAC Nanoflow Lipidomics Workflow

Development and evaluation of an integrated nanoflow lipidomics platform combining the cartridge-based OptiSpray ion source with a 50-cm micro-pillar array column (μPAC). Optimized chromatographic and ionization parameters for maximal lipid coverage and throughput, and benchmarked reproducibility against conventional packed capillary columns. Applied the workflow to generate a reference lipidome atlas across ten mouse tissues from both sexes.

→ In preparation

Species Identification in Ancient Egyptian Archaeological Leather

Used LC–MS/MS paleoproteomics to identify animal species in ancient Egyptian leather from the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Benchmarked three search software packages and two protein databases, with Protein Pilot achieving the highest accuracy (78%). Species assignments were validated by microscopic analysis.

→ npj Heritage Science, 2022

Mentoring Philosophy

The difference between what someone is capable of and what they ultimately achieve often lies in the opportunities they are given to learn.

How I view mentoring. To me, mentoring means opening doors, making difficult concepts approachable, and helping others recognize their potential. Few things are as rewarding as witnessing that “eureka” moment when someone understands something they once found intimidating. My appreciation for education is rooted in my upbringing in Egypt, where access to knowledge and opportunities is not always equal. This taught me that education is not a measure of intelligence, but a means of expanding possibilities across generations and giving people the opportunity to discover what they are good at and what they are passionate about most. Having benefited from educational opportunities myself, I hope to extend them to others.

Ultimately, I hope to be remembered not simply for the knowledge I shared, but for the confidence I helped build and the opportunities I helped create. Perhaps the most beautiful part of mentoring is that learning never flows in just one direction — we set out hoping to make a difference in someone else’s life, and they end up making a difference in ours too.
